insider_note: Writing the equation as dy/dx first and checking that the right side is unchanged when x and y are both scaled by the same number is the fast way to confirm a differential equation is homogeneous before committing to the y = vx substitution.

steps.label: Recognise homogeneous form and substitute
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Every term of the right side has the same total power in x and y (degree 2 over degree 2), so the equation is homogeneous.
steps.memory_tip: Homogeneous means the same total degree on top and bottom — that is the signal to put y = vx.
lines: Put y = vx ⇒ dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx
steps.why: In a homogeneous equation, every occurrence of x and y can be replaced by the single ratio v = y/x, which turns two unknowns into one and makes the equation separable.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the product rule form dy/dx = v + x·dv/dx and writing dy/dx = v instead.
Cancelling x² incorrectly when simplifying (x² + v²x²)/(2x²v).

steps.label: Separate the variables
steps.margin_note: One mark. Move the plain v to the other side before separating x from v.
steps.memory_tip: Isolate x·dv/dx alone on one side, then divide by whatever multiplies it.
steps.why: Once x·dv/dx equals a function of v alone, cross-multiplying puts every v term with dv and every x term with dx, which is the separable form the equation needs before it can be integrated.
common_mistakes: Sign slip when combining 1 + v² − 2v² into 1 − v².
Leaving the equation as x dv = (1 − v²)/(2v) dx instead of separating v to its own side.

steps.label: Integrate both sides
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The left integral is a direct log form once the sign is fixed.
steps.memory_tip: 2v/(1−v²) is minus the derivative of log(1−v²), over its own denominator — a standard log-integral shape.
lines: ⇒ log x + log(1 − v²) = log c
steps.why: The left side is the derivative of −log(1 − v²) with respect to v, since the derivative of the bracket is −2v; the right side is the standard ∫dx/x = log x.
common_mistakes: Missing the minus sign that comes from differentiating (1 − v²).
Writing the constant of integration as a bare c instead of log c, which makes the next line harder to simplify.

steps.label: Return to x and y
steps.margin_note: One mark. Combine the two logs first, then replace v by y/x.
steps.memory_tip: log x + log(1 − v²) = log(x(1 − v²)) — combine before substituting back.
lines: ⇒ log(x(1 − v²)) = log c ⇒ x(1 − v²) = c
Put v = y/x: x(1 − y²/x²) = c
steps.why: Combining the two logs into a single log of a product removes the logs in one step, and only then is it worth substituting v = y/x back in, since the fraction would otherwise need to be carried through the log rule twice.
common_mistakes: Substituting v = y/x too early, before combining the logs, which leads to a messier expression.
Writing v = x/y instead of v = y/x.

steps.label: Final equation
steps.margin_note: The last mark. Clear the fraction 1/x by multiplying through by x.
steps.memory_tip: x(1 − y²/x²) = x − y²/x — multiply by x once more to clear the denominator.
steps.why: Multiplying x − y²/x = c through by x clears the remaining fraction and gives the final relation in whole terms of x and y, which is the form examiners expect as the solution of the differential equation.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as x − y²/x = c instead of clearing the denominator.
Writing the final line as y² − x² = cx, with the sign of the squared terms swapped.
